entries.title: ACTIVATION METHOD
entries.body:
An activation method is the process by which the user community decides on the implementation of a soft fork on the Bitcoin protocol, seeking to avoid a split of the blockchain. This process consists of soliciting the opinion of miners to approve a soft fork before its activation. If a large majority accepts the soft fork, the risk of a blockchain split is minimized. This consensus is crucial because if a majority of miners refuse to make the change, the soft fork could create two distinct chains: one with the modified rules and the other without. There are 2 main categories of activation methods: 
* UASFs (User-Activated Soft Forks) when it is the nodes that enforce the update;
* MASFs (Miner-Activated Soft Forks) when it is the miners who trigger the activation.

There are many different activation methods that have been tested as Bitcoin has evolved. In Satoshi's time, the activation process was not formally established. Changes were often arbitrary and sometimes even made without informing the community. Later, the *Flag Day* method was adopted. After Satoshi's departure, other methods were used successively, notably BIP-0034, BIP-0009, BIP-0008, and finally, *Speedy Trial*.

entries.title: BMM - BLIND MERGED MINING
entries.body: A sidechain consensus technique allowing Bitcoin miners to work simultaneously on the main chain and on one or more sidechains, without having to provide more computational work. Unlike classic merged mining, this method does not require setting up a new node for each sidechain being mined. Within the framework of *Blind Merged Mining* (BMM), each sidechain is managed by independent node operators, responsible for creating blocks and collecting the associated rewards on the sidechain. In return, these operators must buy Proof-of-Work from the miners of the main blockchain in order to validate their blocks on the sidechain. Thus, Bitcoin miners receive their merged mining rewards from the sidechains in BTC, directly on the main chain. This method, developed by Paul Sztorc for drivechains, requires the implementation of BIP-0301 to be operational on the Bitcoin network.

entries.title: ECONOMIC MAJORITY
entries.body: Refers to the largest proportion of the economic activity related to the bitcoin currency, generated by merchants. A merchant is any natural or legal person accepting to exchange a good or a service for BTC. These merchants, which include businesses, users, exchange platforms, and miners, vary in size and economic influence. Some are major players, generating substantial economic activity, while others are more modest. The economic majority is therefore defined by those whose combined economic activity represents the preponderant share of this currency. This majority has an influence on the consensus rules, notably in the event of a fork.

entries.title: GEOMETRIC METHOD
entries.body: A method of calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools. This payment system is based on a score, designed to counter the *pool hopping* phenomenon. It ensures that the payment per submitted share remains constant, regardless of the time of submission. Miners accumulate scores, calculated with a decay factor, and payments are calculated at the end of the cycle. They are proportional to their score. This method involves variable and fixed fees for the miner and reduces the variance of payments per share.

entries.title: LEAD MAINTAINER
entries.body: The lead maintainer was a role within the hierarchy of Bitcoin Core. This role has not existed since February 2023. This person was in charge of leading the project and therefore had more power than the maintainers. The role of lead maintainer was naturally taken on by Satoshi Nakamoto until their departure in early 2011. Subsequently, Gavin Andresen, who had already contributed alongside Satoshi, took over at the head of the software until early 2014. From that date, Wladimir J. van der Laan took on this role until February 2023. Since then, there has been no lead maintainer for the project.

entries.title: M-OF-N
entries.body: Refers to a threshold multisig wallet or script. To strengthen the security of bitcoins, a threshold multisig security system can be used that requires `m` out of `n` signatures to be made in order to spend the funds. In an m-of-n, the letter `m` designates the required signature threshold and the letter `n` designates the total number of existing keys that can sign. For example, in a 2-of-3 configuration, two signatures out of the three possible are required to execute a transaction.

entries.title: MACAROON
entries.body: Authentication mechanism designed to secure access to services on distributed systems. Macaroons are notably used on Lightning to authenticate users when they access delegated services. For example, with a Lightning node, it is possible to generate a macaroon that authorizes transactions to be made from your smartphone via your remote node. Unlike *cookies*, macaroons have the advantage of being cryptographically verifiable by the issuer or of being delegated for verification.

entries.title: MACHANKURA
entries.body: Machankura is a service that allows sending and receiving bitcoins by phone, without an internet connection, thanks to the USSD protocol. Created in 2022 by Kgothatso Ngako, a South African developer, the service makes Bitcoin accessible to users of basic phones in Africa. To make a transaction, the user dials a USSD code specific to their country (for example `*920*8333#` in Ghana) and interacts with a text menu. Payments go through the Lightning Network, and Lightning addresses take the form `numéro@8333.mobi`. Machankura is available in several African countries, including Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa.

entries.title: MAGIC NETWORK
entries.body:
Constants used in the Bitcoin protocol to identify the specific network (mainnet, testnet, regtest...) of a message exchanged between nodes. These values are written at the beginning of each message to make them easier to identify in the data stream. Magic Network values are designed to rarely appear in ordinary communication data. Indeed, these 4 bytes are uncommon in ASCII, are invalid in UTF-8 and generate a very large 32-bit integer, regardless of the data storage format. The Magic Network values are (in *little-endian* format):

Mainnet:
```text
f9beb4d9
```

Testnet:
```text
0b110907
```

Regtest:
```text
fabfb5da
```

*These 4 bytes are sometimes also called "Magic Number", "Magic Bytes" or "Start String".*

entries.title: MAGICAL BITCOIN
entries.body: Former name of the BDK collection of tools and libraries for developers.

entries.title: MAGMA
entries.body:
Liquidity marketplace for the Lightning Network developed by Amboss Technologies. Magma allows node operators to buy or sell inbound capacity in the form of payment channels, regardless of the implementation used (LND, CLN, Eclair).

The mechanism relies on *HODL invoices* to create conditional contracts: the seller only receives payment if they actually open the agreed channel within a short time frame. This system allows Magma to facilitate exchanges without ever taking custody of users' funds.

Magma addresses a recurring need on the Lightning Network: obtaining inbound liquidity. A node that has just opened a channel only has outbound capacity; to receive payments, it must convince a peer to allocate funds on their side of the channel. Magma turns this process into an open market where liquidity is exchanged for fees negotiated between the parties.

entries.title: MAINNET
entries.body: Refers to the main network where real Bitcoin transactions are recorded and executed. The *mainnet* is simply the Bitcoin network. Unlike *testnets*, *regtests* and *signets*, the *mainnet* involves the use of bitcoins that have real economic value.

entries.title: MAINTAINER
entries.body:
In the context of the Bitcoin Core project, the majority node implementation on the Bitcoin network, maintainers are individuals in charge of managing the project. They bear responsibility for the implementation. They are in charge of moderation on the Bitcoin Core GitHub repository and of setting the schedule for the release of new versions. Above all, they are in charge of conducting the merging of *pull requests* (PRs) proposed by contributors. 

In other words, when a proposed code change has passed the various stages of validation, it is these maintainers who bear the great responsibility of merging the new code into the Bitcoin Core software. Before proceeding with this merge, the maintainers check whether the code respects the fundamental principles of the project and whether it has reached the minimum standards required to be included, and they also assess the general consensus of the contributors regarding this change. As I write this definition (March 2026), there are five maintainers on Bitcoin Core: Hennadii Stepanov, Michael Ford, Ava Chow, Ryan Ofsky and Sedited.

entries.title: MARA
entries.body: American Bitcoin mining company listed on the NASDAQ under the symbol MARA. Founded in 2010 and initially active in other sectors, it pivoted to Bitcoin mining starting in 2017, then under the name Marathon Patent Group. In 2021, it was renamed Marathon Digital Holdings, then MARA Holdings in 2024. The company operates data centers in several US states and is among the largest mining companies in the world in terms of hashrate. MARA also operates its own mining pool, MARAPool.

entries.title: MARKET CAP
entries.body: Represents the total value of an asset in circulation, such as bitcoin. It is calculated by multiplying the total number of coins in circulation by the current price of each unit. This figure gives an indication of the overall size and market value of Bitcoin.

entries.title: MASF
entries.body: Acronym for "*Miner-Activated Soft Fork*". Describes a soft fork in Bitcoin when its activation comes from an action by miners. MASFs are a family of soft fork activation methods on Bitcoin. In these approaches, miners signal their agreement and readiness for a protocol update by mining blocks that support the lock-in of the soft fork. If a significant majority of miners votes in favor of the soft fork, the update is considered accepted and is activated later. This process helps avoid splitting the blockchain and maintains the unity of the network. The MASF is preferred for its gentler and more consensual approach, reducing the risk of a blockchain split while ensuring that the majority of computing power supports the new update. The activation methods BIP-0034, BIP-0009, BIP-0008 (if `LOT=false` or if the voting threshold is reached) or Speedy Trial are MASFs.

entries.title: MAST
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Merklized Alternative Script Trees*". A technique employing a Merkle tree to summarize an arbitrary number of user-selected spending conditions in a receiving address, one of which must be fulfilled to spend the bitcoins concerned. The Merkle tree allows the user to choose which condition they wish to fulfill without revealing the details of the other conditions on the blockchain. This makes it possible to reduce the fees associated with these scripts, to create much heavier conditions and, over a longer period, to improve user privacy (in addition to the joint use of Schnorr). This concept was the subject of several proposals, but it was finally added to Bitcoin via the Taproot soft fork in 2021.

*Initially, "MAST" was the acronym for "Merklized Abstract Syntax Tree". The use made of it in the context of Taproot no longer has anything to do with an "Abstract Syntax Tree". However, users continued to use the term MAST. Anthony Towns therefore proposed changing the initial meaning while keeping this widely used acronym with: "Merklized Alternative Script Trees".*

entries.title: MASTER FINGERPRINT
entries.body: 4-byte (32-bit) fingerprint of the master private key in a hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallet. It is obtained by computing the hash `SHA256` of the master private key, followed by a hash `RIPEMD160`, a procedure referred to as `HASH160` on Bitcoin. The Master Fingerprint is used to identify an HD wallet, independently of derivation paths, but taking into account the presence or absence of a passphrase. It is concise information that makes it possible to refer to the origin of a set of keys, without revealing sensitive information about the wallet.

entries.title: MATT
entries.body:
Soft fork proposal whose name stands for "*Merkleize All The Things*" and which aims to introduce covenant capabilities and limited transaction introspection into Bitcoin. MATT was proposed by Salvatore Ingala in 2022.

The core of the proposal relies on the opcode `OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY` (abbreviated `OP_CCV`), which makes it possible to verify that a transaction output commits to a program and to specific data by means of a Merkle tree. Concretely, each state of a contract is represented by a node in a Merkle tree, and the transitions between states are validated by the script itself. This structure makes it possible to verify arbitrary programs in contractual protocols, without requiring a consensus change for each new type of contract.

MATT could enable the implementation of features such as vaults (*vaults*), improved payment channels or other constructions based on covenants. The proposal `OP_VAULT`, which initially aimed at a dedicated vault mechanism, was moreover withdrawn in favor of `OP_CCV`, judged more general-purpose. The opcode was formally integrated into the BIP documentation in 2025.

entries.title: MAX_BLOC_SIZE
entries.body: Constant that specifies the maximum size a block can have on Bitcoin. Historically, this limit was set at 1 MB, a measure put in place by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2010, in order to prevent spam and to maintain a certain decentralization of the network.

entries.title: MAXIMALIST
entries.body: Term that designates a person convinced that Bitcoin is the only cryptocurrency endowed with fundamental value, and that altcoins are superfluous, even harmful. The word comes from the English *Bitcoin maximalist*, an expression coined by Vitalik Buterin in a blog post published in November 2014. Initially used pejoratively to criticize a view of the cryptocurrency ecosystem judged to be narrow, the label was subsequently claimed by those it designated.

entries.title: MEASURE AT THE WALL
entries.body: In the mining industry, refers to measuring the actual electrical consumption of an ASIC directly at its connection point, that is, at the wall power outlet. Unlike theoretical specifications, this measurement makes it possible to precisely quantify the energy consumed by the machine, including all losses during actual operation.

entries.title: MEMPOOL
entries.body:
Contraction of the terms "memory" and "pool". It designates a virtual space in which Bitcoin transactions awaiting inclusion in a block are grouped together. When a transaction is created and broadcast on the Bitcoin network, it is first verified by the nodes of the network. If it is considered valid, it is then placed in the Mempool of each node, where it remains until it is selected by a miner to be included in a block.

It is important to note that each node of the Bitcoin network maintains its own Mempool, and therefore, there may be variations in the content of the Mempool between different nodes at a given time. Notably, the parameter `maxmempool` in the `bitcoin.conf` file of each node allows operators to control the amount of RAM (random access memory) that their node will use to store pending transactions in the Mempool. By limiting the size of the Mempool, node operators can prevent it from consuming too many resources on their system. This parameter is specified in megabytes (MB). The default value of Bitcoin Core to date is 300 MB. 

Transactions present in mempools are provisional. They should not be considered immutable until they are included in a block, and after a certain number of confirmations. They can often be replaced or purged.

entries.title: MEMPOOL.DAT
entries.body: Name of the data file used by the Bitcoin Core software to store the current state of the mempool, which is the set of unconfirmed transactions waiting to be added to a block.

entries.title: MEMPOOL.SPACE
entries.body: Open source block explorer and mempool visualizer for Bitcoin, accessible at mempool.space. This tool makes it possible to consult in real time the state of the mempool (the transactions awaiting confirmation), to estimate optimal transaction fees, to explore blocks, transactions and addresses, and to visualize the state of mining. Mempool.space can also be self-hosted on your own node for sovereign and private use.

entries.title: MERGE
entries.body: In the context of Git, represents the action of integrating the changes from one branch into another, typically bringing the developments of a secondary branch back into the main branch. This operation makes it possible to combine the commit histories of the branches concerned and to resolve any conflicts in order to maintain the integrity of the software.

entries.title: MERKLE BLOCK
entries.body: Data structure used within the framework of BIP-0037 (*Transaction Bloom Filtering*) to provide a compact proof of the inclusion of specific transactions in a block. It is notably used for SPV wallets. The Merkle Block contains the block header, the filtered transactions and a partial Merkle tree, allowing light clients to quickly verify whether a transaction belongs to a block without downloading all the transactions.

entries.title: MERKLE SUM TREE
entries.body: A variant of a Merkle tree in which each node carries not only the hash of the nodes or leaves beneath it, but also the sum of their values. The root of the tree thus contains the hash of all the data and the total sum of all the leaf values. This structure makes it possible to verify both the integrity of the data and the consistency of the amounts at the same time. In the Taproot Assets protocol, *Merkle Sum Trees* are used to commit asset balances to the Bitcoin blockchain, ensuring that no asset can be created or destroyed without changing the root of the tree.

entries.title: METADATA
entries.body: In the general field of computing, this refers to data that provides information about other data. It describes the characteristics, content, quality, format and structure of the data it accompanies. A distinction is thus made between the payload, which represents the core of the information, and the metadata. For example, for a document, the metadata may include the author, the creation date, the file size and the associated keywords. On Bitcoin, metadata can be found in many elements. It is used in receiving addresses, extended keys, blocks...

entries.title: MILLIBITCOIN
entries.body: A subunit of bitcoin equal to one thousandth of a bitcoin, that is 0.001 BTC or 100,000 satoshis. The millibitcoin is sometimes abbreviated as “mBTC”. This unit is used to express intermediate amounts in a more readable way than decimal fractions of a bitcoin, notably in wallet interfaces and exchange platforms.

entries.title: MILLISATOSHI
entries.body: A subunit of the satoshi equal to one thousandth of a satoshi, that is one hundred-billionth of a bitcoin (`10^{-11}` BTC). The millisatoshi does not exist on the Bitcoin blockchain, where the satoshi is the minimum indivisible unit. The Lightning Network, however, uses the millisatoshi as an internal unit of account for payments and the calculation of routing fees, allowing finer granularity.

entries.title: MIMBLEWIMBLE
entries.body:
A protocol that aims to improve the privacy and scalability of transactions. The *white paper* of this protocol was dropped in 2016 on the IRC channel `#bitcoin-wizards` by a user under a pseudonym. Andrew Poelstra then formalized the protocol in a paper published in October 2016. Mimblewimble relies on *Confidential Transactions* and Pedersen commitments to hide amounts, without preventing verification that inputs equal outputs. It uses neither addresses nor a script system: authentication is done solely through the algebraic structure of the transactions. All the transactions in a block are aggregated into a single one, in the manner of a giant *coinjoin*, which makes the links between sender and recipient indistinguishable.

The protocol was implemented in two distinct blockchains launched in January 2019: Grin and Beam. Litecoin integrated an adapted version in the form of extension blocks in May 2022. Mimblewimble has never been integrated into Bitcoin because of its incompatibility with the current script system and UTXO model.

entries.title: MINER
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, a miner refers to a person who operates a mine, that is, a computer engaged in the mining process, which consists of participating in the proof-of-work (*Proof-of-Work*). The miner groups the pending transactions in their mempool to form a candidate block. Then, they search for a valid hash, less than or equal to the target, for the header of this block by modifying the various nonces. If they find a valid hash, they broadcast their block to the Bitcoin network and collect the associated monetary reward, made up of the block subsidy (creation of new bitcoins ex nihilo) and transaction fees.

*In the specific context of mining pools, the role of miner is sometimes distinguished from the role of hasher, given that the individual hashers who take part in the pooling only have to hash and do not take part in the complete process of the mine.*

entries.title: MINIBITS
entries.body: A mobile wallet dedicated to eCash, which uses the Cashu protocol to issue digital tokens backed by bitcoin via the Lightning Network. The application allows payments to be sent and received almost instantly, with a high level of privacy, since eCash transactions are hard to trace.

entries.title: MINING
entries.body:
The act of participating in the proof-of-work (*Proof-of-Work*) of the Bitcoin system. Proof-of-work is a mechanism for resisting Sybil attacks. It is the basis of the Nakamoto consensus mechanism, which is the principle used to establish agreement on a single version of the distributed ledger among the different nodes of the network. 

Concretely, mining is the search for a value that, once passed through a random mathematical function, gives a result below a target number. This proof-of-work target is adjusted every 2016 blocks by the nodes. This is what is called the difficulty adjustment. The target number is lowered to increase the mining difficulty, or raised to decrease the difficulty, depending on the change in the computing power deployed by miners during the previous period. 

![Search for the nonce that produces, via SHA256d on the header, a hash below the target adjusted every 2016 blocks.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/m/minage/assets/image-1.png)

This work done by miners is rewarded with each valid block found. The winning miner collects a monetary reward, made up of the block subsidy (creation of new bitcoins ex nihilo) and transaction fees. Today, the difficulty of proof-of-work on Bitcoin is such that mining requires a great deal of computing power to manage to win blocks. As a result, it is often necessary to have electronic chips specialized in executing `SHA256d`, called ASICs, and to participate in mining pools.

entries.title: MINING MANAGEMENT SOFTWARE
entries.body: Software dedicated to managing and optimizing mining operations. This type of software makes it possible to monitor in real time the performance of ASICs, energy consumption, temperatures, and hash rates. It also offers features for managing large-scale mining farms, with the automation of settings (such as *overclocking*, for example), fault detection and remote management of devices.

entries.title: MINING POOL
entries.body:
Refers to a group of miners who collaborate by combining their computing power to take part in the search for valid Proof-of-Work on Bitcoin. This pooling into a single organization is a solution to the growing difficulty of extracting bitcoins, which makes it too unlikely for an individual miner to compete and win rewards in a stable manner. Miners within a mining pool contribute with their machine to the search for valid shares. When a block is mined by the pool, the reward, which includes the newly created bitcoins as well as the transaction fees included in the block, is distributed among the members of the pool according to the chosen payout method. This distribution is proportional to the computing power that each miner has contributed.

By joining forces, miners within a pool increase their chances of finding blocks and thus reduce their variance. This makes it possible to ensure a more regular and predictable source of income compared to solo mining, where a miner may not win a reward for long periods. They can thus smooth their earnings, and therefore have better visibility on their activity, notably to cope with the various costs it entails.

*Note that the mining pool must not be confused with the mining farm.*

entries.title: MINISCRIPT
MINISKETCH
entries.body:
A set reconciliation library (*set reconciliation*) developed mainly by Pieter Wuille (sipa). Minisketch implements an algorithm that allows two peers in a peer-to-peer network to efficiently determine which elements one has that the other does not, without each having to transmit the complete list of its elements.

The principle relies on sketches (*sketches*): each peer computes a compact representation of its set of elements, whose size depends on the number of expected differences and not on the total size of the sets. By exchanging these sketches, the two peers can identify the missing elements on each side and transmit only those. This mechanism considerably reduces the bandwidth consumed by broadcast protocols (*gossip*).

Minisketch is the fundamental technical building block of Erlay, a proposal to improve transaction relay on the Bitcoin network. Currently, each node announces each transaction to all its peers, which generates significant redundancy. With Erlay, nodes would only announce transactions to a small number of peers, then use reconciliation via Minisketch to synchronize their mempools with the others. This approach could reduce the bandwidth used for transaction announcement by about 84%, and overall bandwidth consumption by about 40%.

entries.title: MINITAPSCRIPT
entries.body:
A version of Miniscript for Tapscript. Tapscript has a few notable differences from Script in its original version. MiniTapscript thus provides support for Tapscript in Miniscript.

*This term is sometimes disputed. Indeed, some bitcoiners prefer to speak of “TapMiniscript”.*

entries.title: MIT DCI
entries.body: A research program of the MIT Media Lab devoted to digital currencies and distributed ledger technologies. Founded in April 2015, this initiative was the first academic group exclusively dedicated to Bitcoin. Its creation came at a time when the Bitcoin Foundation, until then the main source of funding for development, was facing financial difficulties. The DCI funds developers and researchers who work on Bitcoin Core and on the security of the protocol. It thus joins other organizations such as Chaincode Labs, Blockstream or Spiral in supporting the open source development of Bitcoin.

entries.title: MIT X11
entries.body: A very permissive free software license that allows users to copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software. It only requires that the original license and copyright notices be retained in all copies or substantial distributions of the software. Unlike the GPL license, the MIT license does not require that adaptations or derivative versions of the software be distributed under the same license. This flexibility makes the MIT X11 license a popular choice for many *open source* projects, including in the Bitcoin environment. Satoshi Nakamoto, moreover, chose this license for the first version of Bitcoin published in 2009, and it remains in use for the Bitcoin Core project today.

entries.title: MITM - MAN-IN-THE-MIDDLE
frenchAliases: HDM - ATTAQUE DE L'HOMME DU MILIEU
entries.body: An attack in which a malicious actor covertly positions themselves between two communicating parties, in order to intercept and potentially modify the messages exchanged, without the two parties noticing their presence.

entries.title: MIXER
entries.body:
Centralized service that makes it possible to break the history of Bitcoin coins by mixing the funds of several users. Unlike coinjoin, where users retain control of their funds throughout the mixing process, a mixer temporarily takes possession of users' bitcoins, mixes them with those of other users, then sends the funds back to new addresses.

Nowadays, the use of bitcoin mixers is fading in favor of Chaumian coinjoins, which offer more security by eliminating the need for trust. Unlike mixers, where users must entrust their bitcoins to an operator who could steal them or keep data about the mixing process, coinjoins do not present these risks.

entries.title: MIXING
entries.body:
In the general field of mathematics, mixing refers to the property of a dynamical system where, after a certain time, all portions of the initial space can in theory end up mingled with any other portion. Mixing implies that the position of a particle or the state of a system evolves in such a way that its future distribution is independent of its initial distribution, thus reaching a state where the characteristics of the initial state are uniformly distributed throughout the space of the system. In the context of Bitcoin, this notion can be used to evaluate the quality of a coin mixing process such as a coinjoin.

*Some bitcoiners distinguish the notion of mixing from the coinjoin process. Indeed, they say that mixing refers to the mixing of coins carried out by an entity holding the funds, unlike coinjoins where the user always retains possession of the funds. However, in my view, this distinction is incorrect, because coinjoin necessarily involves mixing in the mathematical sense of the term.*

entries.title: MM - MERGED MINING
entries.body: A sidechain consensus technique allowing Bitcoin miners to work simultaneously on the main chain and on one or more sidechains, without having to provide more computational work. It thus involves reusing Bitcoin's Proof-of-Work for third-party applications. However, merged mining has a notable disadvantage for the miner: it requires installing and running node software specific to each sidechain in order to allow the reuse of its Proof-of-Work. In addition, the reward obtained for mining a sidechain is paid on that sidechain and not directly in BTC on the main blockchain.

entries.title: MOSTRO
entries.body: Peer-to-peer bitcoin exchange protocol without KYC, built on Nostr. Mostro makes it possible to buy and sell bitcoins for fiat currencies via the Lightning Network. The protocol uses Lightning *hold invoices* as an escrow mechanism: the seller's bitcoins are locked in a pending invoice and are only released to the buyer after confirmation that the fiat payment has been received. The use of Nostr as a communication layer makes the system censorship-resistant, unlike centralized solutions. Mostro is written in Rust and is open source.

entries.title: MPP - MULTI-PATH PAYMENTS
entries.body:
Generic term for all payment techniques on Lightning that make it possible to split a transaction into several smaller parts and route them via different paths. In other words, each fraction of the payment takes a different path of nodes. This makes it possible to work around liquidity limitations on a single channel in the route.

Multi-path payments also offer slight privacy advantages, because it becomes harder for an observer to link each fraction of the payment to the whole transaction. However, in its basic version, all the fragments share the same secret for the HTLCs, which can make the transaction traceable if an observer is present on several routes. Moreover, because the secret is the same for all the fractions of the payment, the payment is not atomic. This means that some parts of the payment may be executed successfully, while others may fail. These drawbacks are fixed with “*Atomic Multi-Path Payments*”.

*This same method is also sometimes called “Multi-Part Payment”.*

entries.title: MS-SMT
entries.body: The *Merkle Sum Sparse Merkle Tree* (MS-SMT) is a data structure combining the properties of a *Sparse Merkle Tree* (SMT) and a *Merkle Sum Tree*. It makes it possible both to produce proofs of inclusion and non-inclusion (thanks to its “sparse” nature, where each leaf has a position determined by the hash of its key), and to verify the conservation of sums (thanks to the propagation of values in each node up to the root). In the Taproot Assets protocol, the MS-SMT is used to commit assets to the Bitcoin blockchain: its root is embedded in a tapscript of a Taproot transaction. This structure guarantees that it is possible to prove that an asset exists, that an asset does not exist, and that the total of issued assets is consistent, preventing any unauthorized inflation.

entries.title: MTGOX
entries.body: Bitcoin exchange platform founded in 2010 by Jed McCaleb in Tokyo, Japan, then acquired by Mark Karpelès in 2011. At its peak, Mt. Gox handled about 70% of bitcoin transactions worldwide, making it by far the largest exchange platform. In February 2014, Mt. Gox suspended withdrawals and then declared bankruptcy after revealing the loss of about 850,000 bitcoins, 750,000 of which belonged to its customers. The name “Mt. Gox” is an acronym for “Magic: The Gathering Online eXchange”, because the site had originally been designed as a marketplace for cards from that game. This collapse remains one of the most significant events in Bitcoin's history and highlighted the risks of keeping one's bitcoins on a centralized platform.

entries.title: MTP - MEDIAN TIME PAST
entries.body: Concept used in the Bitcoin protocol to determine a margin on the network's consensus timestamp. The MTP is defined as the median of the timestamps of the last 11 mined blocks. Using this indicator avoids disagreements between nodes about the exact time in case of clock offset. The MTP was initially used to verify the validity of block timestamps relative to the past. Since BIP-0113, it is also used as the network's time reference to verify the validity of timelock operations (`nLockTime`, `OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY`, `nSequence` and `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY`).

entries.title: MULTI PROTOCOL COMMITMENT
entries.body: In the RGB protocol, the MPC refers to the Merkle tree structure designed to embed, within a single Bitcoin transaction, several *Transition Bundles* from distinct contracts. This mechanism makes it possible to group various commitments, which correspond to different contracts or assets, into a single anchor point. By consolidating these transitions in a hierarchical structure, the MPC optimizes block space usage, in order to reduce transaction fees and improve the efficiency of blockchain use.

entries.title: MULTISIG
entries.body:
Multisignature wallets, often abbreviated “multisig”, are designed to strengthen the security of bitcoins by requiring several signatures from different private keys to authorize a spend. This method spreads the risk across several keys, which reduces both the risk of loss and that of theft (depending on the multisig configuration). Multisig wallets work according to an “m-of-n” model, where `m` is the minimum number of signatures required to validate a transaction, and `n` the total number of keys involved. For example, a 2-of-3 configuration requires two signatures out of three possible ones to validate a transaction. This approach offers greater security compared to single-key wallets, but it also introduces more complexity in terms of management and backup. Moreover, transactions using the older multisig standards are less private and more expensive in fees than standard *singlesig* transactions. However, recent innovations such as Taproot and the use of *descriptors* will make it possible to minimize, or even eliminate, these drawbacks of multisigs.

*Some bitcoiners distinguish between the terms “Multisig” and “Threshold Multisig”. Indeed, some claim that a multisig is necessarily an n-of-n, whereas a threshold multisig is an m-of-n. However, in everyday language, it is accepted to speak of “Multisig” even for m-of-n.*

entries.title: MUSIG
entries.body:
An n-of-n Schnorr multisignature protocol proposed in 2018 by Gregory Maxwell, Andrew Poelstra, Yannick Seurin and Pieter Wuille. It aggregates the public keys of several signers into a single key and produces a single valid signature, indistinguishable from an individual signature on the blockchain. To counter the rogue key attack (“*rogue key attack*”), in which a participant manipulates their public key to alone control the aggregated key, the protocol multiplies each key by a coefficient derived from the set of keys.

The signing process takes place in three rounds of communication: exchange of cryptographic commitments to the nonces, revelation of the nonces, then exchange of the partial signatures. This three-round structure protects against nonce manipulation attacks, but imposes a constraining interactivity. MuSig has been superseded by MuSig2, which reduces the process to two rounds.

entries.title: MUSIG-DN
entries.body:
A variant of MuSig proposed in 2020 by Jonas Nick, Tim Ruffing, Yannick Seurin and Pieter Wuille. The acronym “DN” stands for “Deterministic Nonces”. The protocol eliminates the nonce commitment round by requiring each signer to derive their nonces deterministically from their private key and the message, then to provide a zero-knowledge proof attesting to the correctness of the computation. This mechanism reduces the signature to two rounds of communication while preventing nonce manipulation.

Despite its theoretical elegance, generating the proofs turns out to be too resource-intensive for practical use, particularly on *hardware wallets*. MuSig-DN remained an intermediate research step and was superseded by MuSig2, which achieves the same two-round goal with a lighter approach based on multiple random nonces.

entries.title: MUSIG2
entries.body:
An evolution of MuSig that reduces from three to two the number of rounds needed to produce an aggregated Schnorr multisignature. Proposed in 2020 by Jonas Nick, Tim Ruffing and Yannick Seurin, the protocol eliminates the nonce commitment round through the use of several random nonces per signer: each participant sends their nonces in the first round, even before knowing the message to sign, then the partial signatures are exchanged in the second round.

Like MuSig, the resulting signature is indistinguishable from an individual signature on the blockchain. However, reusing nonces across signing sessions irreparably compromises the security of the scheme. MuSig2 was formalized in BIP-0327.

entries.title: MYNODE
entries.body: Open source software that makes it easy to deploy a Bitcoin and Lightning full node. MyNode offers an intuitive web interface to manage Bitcoin Core, LND and a set of complementary applications: block explorer, Electrum server, Mempool.space, BTCPay Server, and other tools. MyNode exists in a free version (Community Edition) and a paid version (Premium) with additional features and dedicated support.

entries.title: MYSTERY SHOPPER PAYMENTS
entries.body: An attack in which an attacker sends a small legitimate bitcoin payment to their target in order to obtain information and attempt to compromise their privacy. This technique is often used against merchants. Take the example of Alice, who owns a bakery that accepts bitcoin payments. Eve, the attacker, could buy a croissant to obtain a receiving address from Alice. Eve could then follow the movements of this UTXO to try to deduce additional information about Alice using tracing heuristics.

entries.title: SCRIPT TEMPLATE
entries.body: *Template* allowing the use of standard scripts. A script template is essentially a small list of *opcodes* put together to form a standard that specifies a way of setting spending conditions on bitcoins. Here are some examples of script templates: P2PK, P2PKH, P2WPKH, P2SH...

entries.title: TEMPORAL TEMPLATE
entries.body:
Certain human behaviors are recognizable on-chain. The one that is perhaps the most useful in chain analysis is your sleep rhythm! Yes indeed, when you are asleep, you presumably do not broadcast Bitcoin transactions. And you generally sleep at roughly the same times. It is therefore common to use temporal analysis in chain analysis. It is simply a matter of recording the times at which the transactions of a given entity are broadcast to the Bitcoin network. Analyzing these temporal patterns allows us to deduce a great deal of information. 

First of all, a temporal analysis can sometimes identify the nature of the tracked entity. If we observe that transactions are broadcast steadily over 24 hours, this betrays strong economic activity. The entity behind these transactions is likely a company, potentially international and perhaps with automated internal procedures. On the contrary, if we see that the temporal *pattern* is instead spread over 16 specific hours, then we can estimate that we are dealing with an individual user, or perhaps a local business depending on the volumes exchanged.

Beyond the nature of the observed entity, the temporal *pattern* can also approximately indicate the user's location thanks to time zones. We can then link other transactions, and use their timestamps as an additional heuristic that can be added to a chain analysis.

In a different vein, it is also a temporal analysis of this type that made it possible to formulate the hypothesis that Satoshi Nakamoto was not operating from Japan, but rather from the United States: [_The Time Zones of Satoshi Nakamoto_](https://medium.com/@insearchofsatoshi/the-time-zones-of-satoshi-nakamoto-aa40f035178f).

entries.title: TO MAP
entries.body: In the context of computing, to map refers to the process of associating elements of one dataset with elements of another dataset in a systematic way. This association allows the data of the first set to be substituted for those of the second set or to transition from one to the other. This technique is often used in data transformation operations.

entries.title: TRANSACTION MALLEABILITY
entries.body:
Refers to the possibility of slightly modifying the structure of a Bitcoin transaction, without altering its effect, but while changing the transaction identifier (*TXID*). This property can be exploited maliciously to mislead stakeholders about the status of a transaction, thus causing problems such as double spending. Malleability was made possible by the flexibility of the digital signature used. Malleability notably made an implementation of the Lightning Network complicated. The SegWit soft fork was introduced to solve this problem, by excluding the malleable data of the transaction from the TXID calculation.

*Although it is rare, the term "mutability" is sometimes found to refer to the same concept.*

entries.title: TRANSACTION PATTERN
entries.body:
A transaction *pattern* is simply a typical overall model or structure of a transaction, which can be found on the blockchain, and whose likely interpretation is known and will be useful to us in chain analysis. When studying *patterns*, we focus on a single transaction that we analyze at a high level (as opposed to internal and external chain analysis heuristics). In other words, we will only look at the number of UTXOs as inputs and the number of UTXOs as outputs, without dwelling on more specific details or the environment of the transaction. From the observed pattern, we can interpret the nature of the transaction. We then look for characteristics in its structure and deduce a likely interpretation from them.

*In English, these are called “patterns”.*
